..
Issued at 247 PM CDT Fri Oct 9 2026

Main challenges in the short range will be much above normal 
temperatures, near record levels in fact, along with the combination 
of the stronger wind and low RH values leading to elevated fire 
weather conditions for parts of the CWA through Saturday. Upper flow 
pattern will feature shortwave ridging aloft developing through 
tonight as a southwest flow aloft regime sets up as a western CONUS 
upper trough digs into the Desert SW this weekend into early next 
week. This digging system will eventually lead to noticeable weather 
changes next week compared to our current warm and dry pattern.

High clouds will continue to drift overhead out of MT and ND 
tonight. Low level moisture return on southeast flow this afternoon 
into tonight will continue to advect 50s dewpoints into the forecast 
area. The southeast breezes from the afternoon will diminish a bit 
tonight but remain elevated enough to keep a mild air mass in place. 
Overnight lows in the low to mid 60s for most of our zones will be a 
nice set up to see record warm overnight lows. Sfc low pressure 
tracking out of eastern MT into western ND overnight will help draw 
a warm front through the area enhancing this above normal 
temperature pattern. The sfc low is progged to track northeast 
toward northeast ND on Saturday. A pre-frontal trough will work into 
central SD Saturday morning as a cold front sets up from northeast 
ND into southwest SD by late Saturday afternoon into Saturday night. 
A tight gradient across the region will lead to south to southwest 
wind gusts of 30-40 mph across northeast SD and west central MN 
later tonight through Saturday. A downsloping wind effect will lead 
to locally higher gusts around 45 mph across the eastern slopes of 
the Prairie Coteau late tonight into Saturday. Added patchy blowing 
dust on Saturday to those areas across northeast SD that would be 
most susceptible to the strong winds kicking up dust, especially out 
of agricultural areas.

With a deep south to southwest flow setting up on Saturday across 
the forecast area and a warm air advection regime establishing 925mb 
temps into a +25C to +30C range, daytime readings should have no 
problem reaching the 80s to low 90s. Bumped up these values once 
again closer to the 90th percentile given how anomalous this warm 
air mass will be. The combination of the strong wind and these temps 
will drive RH values down into a 20-25 percent range across central 
SD and a 25-30 percent range from the James Valley and points east. 
The tricky part to the fire weather forecast in this situation is 
winds across central SD are expected to diminish in the afternoon 
while winds across our east remain gusty. So, we have the lowest RH 
in areas with less wind but higher RH values in areas with stronger 
winds. Will have to take this into consideration if conditions 
warrant to issue any fire weather headlines. The strong winds itself 
across our east may be enough to warrant a wind headline, but at 
this time will have incoming shifts have another look at guidance 
tonight and make those decisions. Mainly dry conditions are expected 
through most of the weekend, although can't rule out some shower 
activity entering north central SD the latter half of the weekend or 
certainly by late Sunday.

This will be the beginning signs of changes to come going into early 
next week. That cold front will slowly push east on Sunday into 
Sunday night. Cold air advection could start setting up across north 
central SD as early as late Saturday/early Sunday. Eastern zones 
will hang onto the warmer air mass one more day with highs in the 
70s to low 80s possible across northeast SD and west central MN. 
More widespread rain chances move in by early Monday morning and 
spread east through the day. Lack of any forcing mechanisms should 
lead to more widely scattered light rains with the bulk of any 
precip falling across our northern and western zones. A much cooler 
air mass will infiltrate the area Monday leading to daytime highs 
stuck in the 50s to around 60. Once that upper trough kicks out into 
the central US toward the middle of next week, a better chance for 
more widespread, steadier rainfall can be expected Wednesday into 
Thursday. Temperatures are expected to remain below normal through 
most of the next week with daytime readings in the 50s to mid 60s 
and overnight lows in the 30s and 40s. We might even be cold enough 
with the right conditions setting up late next week for some frost 
into parts of our forecast area.
